options: A number identifying a running process
questions.correctAnswer: A number identifying a running process
questions.explanation:
A PID identifies a process during its lifetime.

Why: Tools use it to inspect or signal a specific running process.

Example: ps displays PIDs beside commands.

Student note: PIDs can be reused after old processes exit, so check what you are targeting.

questions.text: Which tool offers a live view of processes and CPU/memory usage?
questions.explanation:
top refreshes a running view of process/resource usage.

Why: It is useful for finding a process that suddenly consumes CPU.

Example: Sort by CPU to spot a busy service.

Student note: ps provides a snapshot rather than a constantly refreshing view.

questions.text: When an application can shut down cleanly, which signal is normally preferable to start with?
questions.explanation:
SIGTERM requests termination and allows many programs to handle cleanup.

Why: SIGKILL cannot be caught by the application.

Example: kill -TERM 1234 asks the specified process to exit.

Student note: Confirm the PID first, and do not assume the program will obey TERM.

questions.text: Which command displays current services on a systemd-based machine in more detail?
questions.explanation:
systemd-based Linux systems manage service units with systemctl.

Why: Status helps inspect whether a service is active or has failed.

Example: systemctl status nginx can report whether a web server runs.

Student note: Some distributions use service names that differ or another init system.

questions.text: Why use journalctl -u nginx on a systemd-based host?
options: To inspect log entries for the nginx unit
questions.correctAnswer: To inspect log entries for the nginx unit
questions.explanation:
journalctl can query logs collected by systemd-journald.

Why: Filtering with -u focuses on a named service unit.

Example: journalctl -u nginx --since today narrows the investigation.

Student note: Some applications also write separate logs; look for a useful error and time window.

questions.text: What is the purpose of the cron scheduling system?
options: Run specified jobs according to time rules
questions.correctAnswer: Run specified jobs according to time rules
questions.explanation:
A cron job describes a command and when it should run.

Why: It is useful for repeated unattended tasks.

Example: A nightly backup script can have a cron entry.

Student note: Test a script's PATH and permissions because cron's environment differs from an interactive shell.

questions.text: Which command reports active swap areas?
questions.explanation:
Swap is disk-backed backing space available to the memory manager.

Why: swapon --show lists active areas.

Example: free -h also shows a summary of swap use.

Student note: Do not disable swap on a pressured system without understanding the consequences.

questions.text: What is one important difference between df and du?
options: df reports filesystem space; du totals storage used by selected paths
df changes permissions; du changes owner
questions.correctAnswer: df reports filesystem space; du totals storage used by selected paths
questions.explanation:
The tools answer different disk-usage questions.

Why: df checks space on a filesystem, whereas du investigates directories and files.

Example: A filesystem can show full in df, then du can help identify large paths.

Student note: Deleted-but-still-open files can make these reports differ temporarily.

keyTerms.meaning: The tools answer different disk-usage questions.

questions.text: Which command shows block devices with filesystem identifiers useful for mounting?
questions.explanation:
lsblk -f lists block devices and known filesystem metadata.

Why: It helps confirm the partition and UUID before editing mount settings.

Example: Check /dev/sdb1's filesystem type before attempting to mount it.

Student note: Do not guess disk device names on a live machine.

questions.text: Why may an administrator put a UUID rather than a /dev/sdX name in /etc/fstab?
options: UUIDs are generally less sensitive to device-name order changing between boots
It makes data impossible to delete
questions.correctAnswer: UUIDs are generally less sensitive to device-name order changing between boots
questions.explanation:
/etc/fstab can use a filesystem UUID as a stable reference.

Why: Device enumeration such as /dev/sdb can change when disks are added or reordered.

Example: Use blkid to find a UUID before drafting a mount entry.

Student note: A wrong fstab entry can disrupt boot, so validate it safely.

questions.text: What is the main benefit of the directory setgid bit on a collaborative folder?
options: New entries normally inherit the parent directory's group
It gives every user full root privileges
questions.correctAnswer: New entries normally inherit the parent directory's group
questions.explanation:
Shared group inheritance helps files created by different team members remain in a useful group.

Why: A directory with setgid passes its group to new entries in common Linux filesystems.

Example: chmod g+s /srv/team can support collaborative ownership.

Student note: Group inheritance alone does not guarantee write access; check mode bits/default ACL.

questions.text: What does an ACL allow beyond the traditional owner/group/other permissions?
options: Rights for additional named users or groups
questions.correctAnswer: Rights for additional named users or groups
questions.explanation:
Access control lists provide finer-grained permission entries.

Why: For example, one named user can receive access without opening permissions to all others.

Example: getfacl and setfacl inspect and change common POSIX ACLs.

Student note: The ACL mask may limit the effective rights of named entries.

questions.text: Which command normally applies the mode rwxr-x--- to a directory?
questions.explanation:
Numeric mode 750 gives owner 7=rwx, group 5=r-x, others 0=---.

Why: It lets group members traverse/read the directory but not edit its entries.

Example: chmod 750 /srv/reports sets these mode bits.

Student note: To list/traverse a directory correctly, understand read and execute separately.

questions.text: Which statement is most accurate about a backup?
options: A backup needs independent safe storage and a tested recovery procedure
An archive on the same failing disk is always enough
A successful command guarantees future recovery
Backups only matter for source code
questions.correctAnswer: A backup needs independent safe storage and a tested recovery procedure
questions.explanation:
A backup should survive expected failure scenarios and be restorable.

Why: Testing recovery validates that data and procedures are useful.

Example: Store a copy outside the primary machine and practise restoring selected files.

Student note: tar can create archives; it does not by itself establish a complete backup strategy.

study.remember: Testing recovery validates that data and procedures are useful.

questions.text: A server receives an IP address automatically during network startup. Which service commonly provides that configuration?
questions.explanation:
Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol commonly provides network settings to clients.

Why: It may supply IP address, gateway, DNS and—in some PXE settings—boot-related information.

Example: A machine obtains network parameters when joining a managed LAN.

Student note: PXE is a network-boot workflow, not a replacement for DHCP itself.

questions.text: Scenario: After a server reboot, a shared service does not start and staff cannot access a mounted data volume. Outline a safe fault-finding order, including evidence collection and recovery checks.
questions.correctAnswer: Check service status with systemctl and relevant logs with journalctl; inspect mount state with findmnt/mount, block identifiers with lsblk -f or blkid, and available disk/inodes with df -h/df -i; compare /etc/fstab entries with current UUIDs; check permissions; make a backed-up correction, test mount -a where appropriate, restart only after the underlying issue is resolved, and verify service/client access.
aiRubric: Checks actual mounted devices and UUID/fstab consistency
questions.aiReferenceNotes: A service may fail because its data filesystem did not mount or is inaccessible. Record the exact service error and when it began. Verify the device, mount state, capacity and permissions. Correct one known cause at a time and check both mount and service. A stale UUID in fstab could leave /srv/data unmounted, causing the service to fail. Do not format a disk or use chmod 777 as a first troubleshooting step.
questions.explanation:
A service may fail because its data filesystem did not mount or is inaccessible.

Method:
1. Record the exact service error and when it began.
2. Verify the device, mount state, capacity and permissions.
3. Correct one known cause at a time and check both mount and service.

Example: A stale UUID in fstab could leave /srv/data unmounted, causing the service to fail.

Student note: Do not format a disk or use chmod 777 as a first troubleshooting step.

questions.text: Scenario: A company needs nightly backups of a Linux project directory. Design a simple scheduling and recovery plan using standard tools, including how you would know backups really work.
questions.correctAnswer: Choose data scope and frequency, produce dated backups (for example tar or suitable incremental tool), use cron/systemd timers with controlled permissions and logging, store a protected copy off the source disk, monitor for failure, define retention, periodically restore sample files in a safe location, compare expected content and document recovery steps.
aiRubric: Includes secure separate storage and retention
questions.aiReferenceNotes: A backup is valuable only when it can be recovered within the required time. Decide what data is essential and how often it changes. Schedule, protect and record each backup result. Perform and document regular restore tests. A job can use tar to archive /srv/project to a separate destination, followed by a periodic test restore. A green cron exit code alone does not prove that all important files can be restored.
questions.explanation:
A backup is valuable only when it can be recovered within the required time.

Method:
1. Decide what data is essential and how often it changes.
2. Schedule, protect and record each backup result.
3. Perform and document regular restore tests.

Example: A job can use tar to archive /srv/project to a separate destination, followed by a periodic test restore.

Student note: A green cron exit code alone does not prove that all important files can be restored.
